euro.e: The name euro was the winner of a contest open to the general public to propose names for the new European currency, and as such is technically a neologism, although it obviously alludes to the common root of geographical names for the continent Europe, derived from Latin Europa, from Ancient Greek Εὐρώπη (Eurṓpē), the name in Greek mythology of a princess, abducted by Zeus as a bull across the Bosporus. According to the official story, the term was coined by Belgian teacher and esperantist Germ

s.d: the basic monetary unit of most members of the European Union (introduced in 1999); in 2002 twelve European nations (Germany, France, Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Italy, Spain, Portugal, Ireland, Greece, Austria, Finland) adopted the euro as their basic unit of money and abandoned their traditional currencies
The currency unit of the European Monetary Union. Symbol: €
A coin with a face value of one euro.
Any member of the species Macropus robustus of macropods; a wallaroo.
The UEFA European Football Championship, a European football competition held between the international teams of Europe every four years.
Electronic trance from Europe.
x: Euro-Trance emerged as a hybrid of Hard Trance and Eurodance music and was most popular between late 1998 and 2000.

s.d: admiration for Europe, Europeans, or the European Union.
x: The other challenge is that this open and liberal Euroscepticism may be an even more elite project than liberal Europhilia.

s.d: (uncountable) The love of Europe, Europeans, or European culture.

eurythmy.e: From Ancient Greek εὐρυθμία (euruthmía, “rhythmical order”), from εὖ (eû, “well”) + ῥυθμός (rhuthmós, “symmetry”).

(uncountable) The harmony of features and proportion in architecture.
(uncountable) Graceful body movements to the rhythm of spoken words and music.
x: For three weeks Lorde engages in a regime of rest, relaxation, eurhythmy, and active meditation.

s.d: (uncountable) Healthy, normal beating of the pulse; eurhythmia.

s.d: a sporangium that arises from a group of epidermal cells

eutectic.e: From Ancient Greek εὔτηκτος (eútēktos, “easily melted”), from εὖ (eû, “well”) + τήκω (tḗkō, “to melt”). Coined as an adjective (along with the noun eutexia) by British scientist Frederick Guthrie in 1884.

s.d: a mixture of substances having a minimum melting point
A material that has the composition of a eutectic mixture or eutectic alloy.
The temperature of the eutectic point.

Describing the chemical composition or temperature of a mixture of substances that gives the lowest temperature at which the mixture becomes fully molten. A further requirement is that that temperature is lower than the melting point of any of the pure component substances.
Describing the thermodynamic equilibrium conditions where a liquid coexists with two solid phases.
x: For a mixture with two components at a fixed pressure, the eutectic reaction can only happen at a fixed chemical composition and temperature, called the eutectic point.

s.d: a steel that contains 0.9% carbon (the eutectic point); a carbon steel with 0.9% carbon is pure pearlite

euthanasia.e: First attested in 1606, from Ancient Greek εὐθανασία (euthanasía), from εὐ- (eu-, “good”) + θάνατος (thánatos, “death”)

s.d: the act of killing someone painlessly (especially someone suffering from an incurable illness)
(uncountable) The practice of intentionally killing a human being or animal in a humane way, especially in order to end suffering.
x: Euthanasia is the most difficult part of a veterinarian's job.
In recent years, the sisters spoke openly about their desire for euthanasia in the event that one of them became gravely ill.

s.d: (euphemistic, uncountable) The practice of killing a human being who is considered a liability to society, especially a disabled person.
(obsolete, uncountable) An easy death, or the means to bring about such a death.
x: For myself I could hold it in my account with God to find such an euthanasia for you, even at this moment if it were best.

euthanatize.e: From euthanasia + -ize, euthanat- being the stem of euthanasia.

s.d: intentionally cause the painless death of a person or animal
To euthanize.
intentionally cause the painless death of a person or animal
To carry out euthanasia on (a person or animal).
x: John decided to euthanize his dying dog.
A terminally ill minor has become the first child to be euthanized in Belgium since age restrictions were lifted in the country two years ago.

s.d: the study of methods of improving human well-being and efficient functioning by improving environmental conditions
(uncountable) The study of the effects of place on people.
(uncountable) The study of improvement of human function when their environment improves.

eutrophic.e: From Ancient Greek εὖ (eû) + τροφικός (trophikós), literally “well-nourished”; equivalent to eu- + trophic.

s.d: A eutrophic medicine.
(ecology) of a lake or other body of water rich in nutrients and subject to eutrophication
Being rich in nutrients and minerals and therefore having an excessive growth of algae and thus a diminished oxygen content to the detriment of other organisms.
Promoting nutrition.

x: he argued that the controlling factor in eutrophication is not nitrate but phosphate

x: Amphisteginids and peneroplids were among the few taxa found in the bay environments, probably due to their preferences for phytal substrates and tolerance to moderate levels of eutrophication.
